P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes, freely. Djibouti has no foreign-exchange restrictions: no limits on converting or transferring funds, or on money flowing in and out. The Djibouti franc has been pegged to the US dollar under a currency board since 1949 (DJF 177.7 per USD) and is freely convertible.

P3_local_gateways.question: Which local payment gateways can an individual or sole trader use to accept online payments?
P3_local_gateways.answer: Global platform availability for Djibouti (automated collector snapshots, Oct 2026). Available: Paddle (not on its exclusion list; software sellers only, each seller reviewed); Whop (payouts); Dodo Payments (sellers); Google Play (developer registration). Not listed: Stripe (merchant sign-up); Lemon Squeezy payouts; Polar (payouts); Etsy seller payments; YouTube Partner Program.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: Partly established. All individuals in commerce, industry or any profession, nationals or foreigners, must pay the annual business licence fee (patente), renewable each year, subject to exemptions in the General Tax Code. The one-stop registration procedure for an individual business was not captured.
L1_registration.note: Single secondary domain (Oxford Business Group 2023); ANPI one-stop shop not captured on 2026-10-22.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Partly established. For business profits, resident and non-resident entities are taxed only on income from activities carried out in Djibouti (territorial), at 25% of net profit or 1% of turnover. Personal income tax for individual businesses and the forfait regime were not captured.
L3_income_tax_foreign.note: Single secondary domain (OBG 2023), and the territoriality quote refers to CIT entities; individual regime not captured on 2026-10-22.

sources.quote: Corporate Income Tax (CIT) Resident and non-resident entities are subject to CIT only on income generated from activities carried out in Djibouti.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: Standard VAT 10%. Businesses with turnover between DJF 10m and 20m (depending on activity) must register; exports and international transport are exempt (Oxford Business Group, 2023). Later finance-law changes were not checked.
L4_vat_gst.note: Single secondary domain (OBG 2023) on 2026-10-22; CGI/finance law not read.

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: Djibouti adopted its first Digital Code (Code du Numérique) on 30 June 2025, covering personal data protection (Book One), cybersecurity and e-commerce. The National Commission for the Protection of Personal Data it provides for was listed as not yet established.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: Stripe does not accept merchants here; platforms that pay out through PayPal Payouts cannot pay PayPal accounts here (not on PayPal's Payouts list, see P4 for ordinary PayPal receiving); Wise does not let residents hold money. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
